stories.headline: Nearly 2,000 Boeing 737s Must Get Tail Inspections After Jets Pitched Up And Down Mid-Flight
stories.claim: FAA orders tail inspections on nearly 2,000 US-registered Boeing 737NG jets over horizontal stabilizer freeplay.
stories.summary: The US Federal Aviation Administration has issued an airworthiness directive requiring inspections of 1,987 US-registered Boeing 737NG aircraft. The checks look for excessive freeplay in the horizontal stabilizer hinges and jackscrew, which could lead to flutter and loss of control if not fixed. The directive takes effect on 23 November and follows several reports of pitch oscillation events, though the FAA did not give details of the incidents. Airlines including United and Alaska asked for more time or flexibility, but the FAA rejected those requests. Each inspection is estimated to cost about $510 per aircraft, with more than $1 million across the US fleet, excluding parts.
key_points: The FAA has ordered inspections of 1,987 US-registered 737NG aircraft.
The directive, AD 2026-20-14, takes effect on 23 November.
Checks target excess freeplay at the stabilizer hinges and jackscrew, following pitch oscillation reports.
The FAA rejected airline requests for longer intervals and more flexibility.
Estimated cost is about $510 per aircraft, over $1 million across the US fleet before parts.
The directive does not cover the 737 MAX and applies to US-registered aircraft only.
stories.market_take: Modest effect expected, mainly on maintenance costs for affected airlines and Boeing's aftermarket business.

stories.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the Sunday Times he would welcome an honest, evidence-based discussion about returning to EU free movement, potentially as part of a new relationship that could include single market membership. He ruled out joining the euro or Schengen. Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said there could be no return to free movement, while Reform UK leader Nigel Farage called the remarks a betrayal of Brexit voters. Burnham has previously said that Labour's 2024 manifesto ruled out free movement, single market membership and a customs union, and that fundamental changes would need a general election mandate. He is expected to pitch options for a reset of relations at an EU summit in Brussels on 20 November.
key_points: Burnham says he wants an evidence-based debate on free movement, which could be part of a closer EU relationship.
He said migration under EU membership was different, as it involved younger people spending a few years and then returning.

stories.headline: AI panic and market volatility: Are the stock market’s big gains unsustainable?

stories.summary: An NPR interview with senior business editor Rafael Nam looks at why US stock markets have been volatile in 2026 despite strong gains over the past four years. The Nasdaq suffered its biggest one-day loss in months earlier this week, with AI concerns a major factor. Other pressures include a war with Iran driving energy prices higher, and the Federal Reserve raising interest rates. Meta's announcement that it would need to raise more money for AI hit its shares and weighed on the wider market on Thursday. A CalPERS pension fund is reportedly shifting some investments away from big tech to reduce concentration risk, and experts advise diversification.

stories.headline: Bipartisan US Lawmakers Push Back On Trump's Russia Policy, Vow Support For Ukraine
stories.claim: Bipartisan US lawmakers push back on Trump's Russia diesel waiver and demand guaranteed Ukraine access to Starlink and military support.
stories.summary: A bipartisan group of US lawmakers is challenging the Trump administration's decision to authorise transactions involving Russian diesel, issued by a Treasury waiver on October 9. Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, with Republican Don Bacon and Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, has introduced the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act of 2026 to nullify the waiver and ban future Russian energy waivers. Separately, eight lawmakers from both chambers urged Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to expand the Starshield contract and guarantee uninterrupted Starlink and Starshield access for Ukraine. The pushback follows reported disruptions to Ukraine's satellite communications, which Kyiv said had been restored on October 24. The bill has been referred to three House committees.

stories.headline: Turkey's new deal on Mediterranean maritime boundaries with Libya is exacerbating issues with Greece and the EU
stories.claim: Libya's eastern parliament approved a maritime deal with Turkey, drawing rejection from Greece and criticism from the EU.
stories.summary: Libya's parliament unanimously approved a maritime agreement with Turkey that creates a direct economic corridor between the two countries' coasts. The eastern parliament reversed its earlier opposition to a 2019 deal first agreed with the UN-recognised government in western Libya. Greece says the corridor disregards Crete, Karpathos and Rhodes and has rejected the accord, with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas saying it infringes the sovereign rights of third states. The area is believed to hold gas reserves worth several hundred billion dollars. The deal also cuts across the planned EastMed pipeline, and analysts see a possible split of the eastern Mediterranean into rival blocs.

The corridor links southern Turkey and northern Libya and overlaps with areas Greece claims under its exclusive economic zone.

stories.headline: Violence, intimidation and fear: 10 years on from the ‘Jungle’, life in Calais migrant camps is harsher than ever
stories.claim: A decade after the Calais Jungle was demolished, migrants face harsher conditions, evictions and intimidation.
stories.summary: Ten years after the demolition of the Calais Jungle, around 4,000 asylum seekers remain in smaller camps across Calais, Dunkirk and Boulogne. Conditions are described as harsher, with small camps evicted roughly every 48 hours and police accused of increased violence. Small boat arrivals to the UK have fallen from over 41,000 in 2025 to about 21,000 so far this year, though officials attribute part of this to fewer crossings across Europe and windy weather. Charities report rising police violence and far-right harassment, and the National Crime Agency says smuggling business models are starting to shake.

stories.headline: Music streaming: Why we're listening to so many old songs
stories.claim: Most music listening is now to older songs, with classics dominating streams as AI and volume of new releases grow.

The Competition and Markets Authority notes that nearly two thirds of streams go to the top 0.4% of artists, which makes it hard for emerging acts to sustain careers. stories.claim: Researchers modelled the Martian Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud, suggesting homogeneous nucleation driven by unobserved physics.
stories.summary: Researchers led by Jorge Hernández-Bernal of Sorbonne Université have modelled the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud on Mars for the first time. The cloud appears each Martian spring and summer near the volcano Arsia Mons, stretching over 1,000 miles before dissipating. The simulations suggest it forms through homogeneous nucleation, where vapour turns directly into ice without dust particles, a process not yet observed on any planet. Reproducing the cloud required a sharp temperature drop of 30°C within 10 minutes and extreme humidity, far above any value measured on Earth. The study was published in Nature Geoscience.

stories.headline: CFTC Charts Federal Path for Retail Crypto Transactions and Cryptoasset Markets
stories.claim: The CFTC has issued a proposal that could bring leveraged and fully paid retail crypto trades under its regulation.
stories.summary: The US Commodity Futures Trading Commission has issued an advance notice of proposed rulemaking setting out a possible federal framework for retail crypto transactions. It proposes two rules, Regulation CTX and Regulation CAM, and uses Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act as the legal basis. A key preliminary view is that a platform-wide offer of leverage could bring even fully paid crypto purchases under CFTC oversight. If a platform registers as a designated contract market, it would also be preempted from state money-transmitter laws, according to the Commission's preliminary view. The document is a request for public comment and contains no draft regulatory text.

It proposes Regulation CTX and Regulation CAM under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the CEA.

Exchanges would need designated contract market status, with state money-transmitter laws preempted in the Commission's view.
The notice seeks public comment and does not yet include proposed rule text.

Taiwan's Central Weather Administration said the system was weakening, with gusts of around 126km/h near its centre, and it was about 150km east of the island. Northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, extended office and school closures for a second day and some flights were still cancelled. The storm is forecast to turn north towards China's coast and later move into southern Japan.

stories.headline: Major US banks are locking out AI agents that log in with customer credentials
stories.claim: Major US banks are restricting third-party AI agents that log in using customer credentials, with some blocking them entirely.
stories.summary: Several large US banks, including Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, Bank of America, Citi and Wells Fargo, are restricting external AI agents from accessing customer accounts, according to a report by Axios. The agents are using customer-provided login details, which breaches bank policies that require account holders to log in personally. Some agents appear to act without direct user instructions. Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan reportedly block agents entirely, while most banks want to allow only read-only access. Banks say security risks are too high for now, and many cannot tell whether an agent is acting for a user or on its own. Blocking such access on the provider side will be difficult, since users can connect agents through browsers or open-source tools. OpenAI has launched a read-only ChatGPT service for financial tasks in the US.

stories.headline: Etsy is cracking down on AI slop listings
stories.claim: Etsy is introducing stricter rules on AI-generated content in listings, including a requirement for an unedited first photo.
stories.summary: Etsy has announced tighter rules on the use of AI in listings, aiming to cut down on low-quality AI-generated items, or 'AI slop', on its platform. Every listing must include at least one unedited photo of the real item against a real background, and all photos must accurately represent what the buyer receives. Sellers must disclose AI-made images when prompted, and the seller may face a refund liability if a buyer reports the item is materially different. Sellers of patterns, recipes and guides must write them themselves and show an actual result. Bot-made listings are banned, but AI-generated art is still allowed if disclosed.

stories.headline: Hoka and Ugg Parent Deckers Brands Sees Shares Fall After Q2 Sales Miss

stories.headline: Woman 'scared to turn heating on' due to oil cost
stories.claim: Rural households reliant on heating oil face sharp price rises, prompting councils to offer crisis funds.
stories.summary: A 76-year-old pensioner in Yealmpton, south Devon, says she is afraid to switch on her heating because the price of domestic heating oil has nearly doubled. She says 500 litres that cost £317 plus VAT about six months ago would now cost £600 plus VAT. The BBC reports that heating fuel costs have risen by up to 82% since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, according to the energy consumers minister. The government recently promised tighter regulation of the sector, and Cornwall and Devon councils have crisis resilience funds to help struggling households. The story highlights the strain on off-grid households in rural areas.
key_points: A Devon pensioner says the cost of heating oil has nearly doubled, leaving her afraid to use her heating.
500 litres of oil rose from £317 plus VAT to £600 plus VAT in about six months.
The minister says heating fuel costs have risen by up to 82% since the Iran war began.
The government has promised tighter regulation, competition measures and clearer compensation routes for customers.
Cornwall and Devon councils are offering crisis resilience funds to eligible low-income households.
stories.market_take: Limited direct market effect; mainly a consumer cost-of-living story.

stories.headline: Sainsbury’s warns on ‘tough’ trading conditions as sales growth slows
stories.claim: Sainsbury's raised its full-year profit target as like-for-like sales growth slowed and it warned of tough trading conditions.
stories.summary: Sainsbury's lifted the lower end of its full-year underlying profit target to £1.025bn from £965m, with an upper range of £1.065bn, even as like-for-like sales growth slowed to 1.2% in the three months to September from 2.3%. Chief executive Simon Roberts warned that many households are finding things tough. Its premium Taste the Difference range is growing strongly. The company reported a £164m pre-tax loss in the first half, largely due to the Argos sale to Swift Partners for £120m, though underlying pre-tax profit rose 5% to £366m. Market share slipped to 15.2%, behind Tesco on 27.8%, and the grocer had earlier held merger talks with Morrisons, which were abandoned in February.
key_points: Sainsbury's raised the lower end of its full-year profit target to £1.025bn, with an upper range of £1.065bn.
Like-for-like sales growth slowed to 1.2% in the three months to September, from 2.3%.
Grocery sales growth slowed to 2.2%, while general merchandise and clothing improved.
The Argos sale to Swift Partners for £120m led to a £164m pre-tax loss in the first half.
Market share fell to 15.2%, according to Worldpanel, behind Tesco on 27.8%.
Food inflation is expected to exceed 6% by July next year because of energy and supply costs linked to the Iran war.
stories.market_take: Raised profit guidance is supportive, but slowing sales and tougher conditions weigh on the outlook for UK grocers.

stories.headline: China seeks to seize 61,800 BTC tied to $5.7 billion fraud scheme
stories.claim: Chinese prosecutors moved to confiscate over 61,800 bitcoin linked to a 40 billion yuan fraud case.
stories.summary: Chinese prosecutors have asked a Tianjin court to confiscate more than 61,800 bitcoin, worth roughly $5.7 billion, linked to a large fraud. The case centres on Qian Zhimin, who allegedly ran Tianjin Lantian Gree Electronic Technology, which raised over 40 billion yuan from more than 102,000 investors through unlicensed wealth products between 2014 and 2017. The court accepted the request on 13 October and opened a six-month period for victims to join the case. The bitcoin was seized in the UK, and a UK High Court recently ruled that Chinese law should govern victims' claims.
key_points: Prosecutors seek to confiscate more than 61,800 bitcoin, worth about $5.7 billion, tied to the fraud case.
The alleged scheme raised over 40.378 billion yuan from more than 102,000 investors, who lost nearly 20 billion yuan.
Qian Zhimin fled China in 2017 and later settled in the UK, where British authorities seized his assets.
Tianjin's Second Intermediate People's Court accepted the request on 13 October and opened a six-month window for claimants.
A UK High Court ruling said Chinese law should govern the victims' claims, and further hearings are expected.
Some victims' lawyers are seeking to appeal that ruling.
stories.market_take: A large sale or transfer of seized bitcoin could add supply sentiment, though the timeline is uncertain.
